scenes.text: How behind are you really? Median net worth in Canada under 35
How behind are you really? Median net worth in Canada under 35

script.caption:
That $159,100 number made me feel broke too, until I looked at where it comes from.

It's Statistics Canada's median net worth for households where the main earner is under 35 (2023 data). But it includes everyone who already owns a home, and young homeowners have a median of $457,100, mostly from their house.

If you rent, the median is $44,000. If you rent and don't have a work pension, it's $27,000. That's where most people our age actually are.

What actually moves your number in your 20s:
1. A $2,000 emergency fund, so a surprise bill doesn't go on a card at 20% (Saved: ~$150/mo)
2. Paying off anything with a high interest rate
3. Putting a set amount into your TFSA every payday, even $50 (Saved: ~$100/mo)

scenes.text: How to stop bleeding $800 a month on accidental food spending
How to stop bleeding $800 a month on accidental food spending

script.caption:
$15 lunch, $6 coffee, a $6 snack in the afternoon. That's $27.40 a day without trying, which is $833 a month and just over $10,000 a year.

I'm not saying never buy lunch. I'm saying most of those days I didn't even want it, I just didn't bring anything.

What fixed it for me:
1. Cook once on Sunday (Saved: ~$250/mo)
Rice, chicken, roasted veggies, 45 minutes. That covers 4 lunches.

2. Keep snacks in your bag or desk (Saved: ~$80/mo)
A box of granola bars costs less than two café snacks.

3. Make coffee at home (Saved: ~$100/mo)
Buy the café one on Fridays.

And if you put that $833 a month into an index fund instead, at 8% a year it'd be around $150,000 after 10 years. Not guaranteed, but that's the math.

scenes.text: Skipping lattes won't get you to a 50% savings rate. These 5 things will.
Skipping lattes won't get you to a 50% savings rate. These 5 things will.

script.caption:
Everyone wants to talk about your $6 latte. It barely matters. If you want to save half your income, it comes down to a few big decisions.

1. Don't finance a car you can't pay off (Saved: ~$600/mo)
A new car payment can easily hit $600 to $700 a month. A used car you own outright, or transit, keeps that money yours.

2. Move half your pay on payday (Saved: ~$500/mo)
Set up an automatic transfer for the morning your paycheque lands. You can't spend what's already gone.

3. Keep rent under 25% of what you take home (Saved: ~$400/mo)
Roommates aren't fun forever, but they're the fastest way to free up cash in your 20s.

4. Get a raise, keep your life the same (Saved: ~$200/mo)
Same apartment, same phone, same car. The new money goes straight to savings.

5. Spend on skills, not stuff (Saved: ~$300/mo)
A course or certification that bumps your pay by $10k does more than any amount of coupon clipping.

scenes.text: How to build a $5,000 emergency fund from $0 this year
How to build a $5,000 emergency fund from $0 this year

script.caption:
Assuming your paycheque will always be there is how people end up in trouble. Layoffs, cut hours, a contract that doesn't get renewed. It happens to a lot of people in their 20s.

Here's how I'd build a 6-month emergency fund from zero:

1. Figure out your bare minimum
Rent, groceries, phone, transit, minimum debt payments. Nothing else. Times 6 is your goal.

2. Get to $1,500 first (Saved: ~$300/mo)
Pause extra spending for a few weeks until you have $1,500. That covers most car repairs and dentist bills without a credit card.

3. Keep it at a different bank (Saved: ~$150/mo)
Open a HISA somewhere you don't do your everyday banking. It takes a day or two to move money back, which is enough to stop you from dipping into it.

4. Treat it like a bill (Saved: ~$200/mo)
Automatic transfer every payday, same as rent.

Daily savings breakdown to afford your biggest goals in 1 year

Europe trip, $4,000: $10.96 a day, about $333 a month
Pack lunch twice a week and make coffee at home and you're most of the way there.

Car down payment, $7,000: $19.18 a day, about $583 a month
Cut eating out in half and cancel the subscriptions you forgot about.

Wedding or ring, $12,000: $32.88 a day, $1,000 a month
This one needs your tax refund, bonuses or side income, not just cutting back.

House fund, $25,000: $68.49 a day, about $2,083 a month
Honestly this takes more than a year for most people, and that's fine. If you're a first-time buyer, look into the FHSA.

scenes.text: In debt? Do these 5 things this week
In debt? Do these 5 things this week

script.caption:
Debt feels way worse when it's a blur. Once it's written down, it's just a plan.

1. Write down every balance
Every card, loan and line of credit. Balance, interest rate, minimum payment. One list.

2. Pick one to attack (Saved: ~$150/mo in momentum)
Pay the minimum on everything and put every extra dollar on one debt. Smallest balance first gets you a quick win (snowball). Highest interest first saves the most money (avalanche). Both work.

3. Keep $1,000 in cash (Saved: ~$100/mo)
Without a buffer, the next surprise bill goes right back on the card.

4. Take your card off your phone (Saved: ~$150/mo)
Delete it from Apple Pay and every saved checkout. Having to dig out your wallet stops a lot of impulse buys.

5. Every windfall goes to the debt (Saved: ~$200/mo)
Tax refund, bonus, money from selling old stuff on Marketplace. Straight to the target balance.

While you build that $1,000, check out Lodavo. Every $25 you keep saved is a ticket in a weekly cash draw, so building the buffer is a bit more fun. Free, link in bio.

scenes.text: 5 things I'll never cheap out on (and what I cut instead)
5 things I'll never cheap out on (and what I cut instead)

script.caption:
Saving money doesn't mean cutting everything. I spend on what I care about and I'm cheap about the rest.

1. Dinner with family, not bar rounds (Saved: ~$200/mo)
I'll happily pay for dinner with my parents. I won't spend $80 buying rounds at a crowded bar.

2. A good mattress, not new clothes every month (Saved: ~$150/mo)
I sleep on it every night. The fast-fashion shirt I wore twice, not so much.

3. Courses and tools that make me money, not 4 streaming services (Saved: ~$60/mo)
If it helps me earn more, I'll pay for it. If I haven't opened it in a month, it's cancelled.

4. Good groceries, not delivery (Saved: ~$250/mo)
Real food from the store is cheaper than Uber Eats and I feel better eating it. I'm done paying delivery fees.

5. A reliable car, not a new one (Saved: ~$150/mo)
I want it to start every morning. I don't need this year's model.

scenes.text: 4 ways to cut $400 a month off your food spending (without eating rice every night)
4 ways to cut $400 a month off your food spending (without eating rice every night)

script.caption:
Food is where most of my money was going and I didn't even notice. You don't need to starve to fix it.

1. Keep "lazy meals" in the freezer (Saved: ~$150/mo)
Frozen pizza, dumplings, chicken strips. The night you're too tired to cook, you make that instead of a $35 Uber Eats order.

2. Shop the outside of the store (Saved: ~$120/mo)
Produce, meat, dairy. The middle aisles are mostly expensive snacks.

3. Build meals on cheap staples (Saved: ~$80/mo)
Rice, pasta, potatoes, oats. Spend the money on good protein and a sauce you like.

4. Go out for lunch, not dinner (Saved: ~$60/mo)
A lot of restaurants have lunch prices that are 20 to 30% cheaper for basically the same food.

scenes.text: Money habits I wish I started at 17 (they add up to $10,000 a year)
Money habits I wish I started at 17 (they add up to $10,000 a year)

script.caption:
Nobody taught me this in high school, so here's what I'd tell 17-year-old me.

1. Save 20% of every paycheque automatically (Saved: ~$400/mo)
Set the transfer for payday morning. You get used to the rest fast.

2. Buy refurbished tech (Saved: ~$100/mo)
Certified refurbished phones and laptops come with a warranty and cost way less than new.

3. Wait 48 hours before buying online (Saved: ~$150/mo)
Put it in your cart, close the app. Most of the time you forget about it.

4. Bring lunch to work or school (Saved: ~$200/mo)
Leftovers or a sandwich instead of $15 takeout.

5. Call your phone and internet company once a year (Saved: ~$50/mo)
Ask what deals they have. Mention a competitor's price. It works more than you'd think.

That's about $900 a month, or over $10,000 a year.

scenes.text: Free money a lot of Canadians in their 20s never claim
Free money a lot of Canadians in their 20s never claim

script.caption:
Most people our age leave money on the table just because nobody told them.

1. File your taxes, even if you barely made anything
You have to file to get the GST/HST credit, which is paid every 3 months if your income is low.

2. Your province might pay you too
The Ontario Trillium Benefit and Quebec's solidarity tax credit both need a tax return.

3. Don't throw away your tuition slip
Your T2202 gets you a federal tuition credit. If you don't need it this year, it carries forward to when you earn more.

4. Take the employer match
If your job matches RRSP or pension contributions and you're not signed up, you're turning down part of your pay.

5. Student pricing
UNiDAYS, Spotify Premium Student, Amazon Prime Student. Use them while you can.

scenes.text: HISA vs TFSA vs FHSA, explained in 15 seconds
HISA vs TFSA vs FHSA, explained in 15 seconds

script.caption:
Confused by all the acronyms? Same. Here's the short version.

HISA (high-interest savings account)
Cash that earns some interest. Good for your emergency fund and short-term goals. The interest is taxed unless it's inside a TFSA.

TFSA (Tax-Free Savings Account)
Not just a savings account. You can hold cash, index funds or ETFs, and anything it earns is tax-free. You get new room every year starting the year you turn 18.

FHSA (First Home Savings Account)
Only for first-time buyers. Up to $8,000 a year, $40,000 total. You get a tax deduction going in, and it comes out tax-free when you buy your first home.

What I'd do: emergency fund in a HISA first, then the FHSA if you want to buy a home, then the TFSA.
